title: Tourniquet in Cardiopulmonary Resuscitation (T-CPR) – Use of Tourniquets During Cardiopulmonary Resuscitation
summary:
Study Goal
The aim of this study is to improve blood pressure during resuscitation in patients who suffer a cardiac arrest and are brought to the intensive care unit while CPR is still ongoing. To do this, special bands (similar to those used during a blood draw) are placed around the arms and legs to help push blood toward the heart, brain, and lungs – a technique known as autotransfusion.

Despite progress in emergency medicine, cardiac arrest outside the hospital (called out-of-hospital cardiac arrest, or OHCA) remains extremely dangerous. Many patients don’t survive, and among those who do, only a small number retain good brain function.

Drugs like adrenaline (epinephrine) can help restart the heart, but they don’t always protect the brain. One reason might be that, while adrenaline increases blood pressure, it may also narrow small blood vessels in the brain, possibly reducing oxygen supply to brain tissue.

A promising new technique is called Tourniquet-CPR (T-CPR). During resuscitation, bands are applied to the arms and legs – similar to a tourniquet – to keep more blood in the central part of the body. This may help send more blood and oxygen to the brain and heart.

Early results from animal studies and small human pilot studies are encouraging:
Blood pressure in key vessels increases,
Brain blood flow improves,
The chances of restarting the heart (return of circulation) go up,
And there were no signs of long-term damage to the arms or legs caused by the bands.

So far, there are no large clinical studies in humans to prove that T-CPR is both effective and safe. But the early findings are hopeful. T-CPR could potentially improve survival after cardiac arrest – and protect brain function in survivors.

interventions.name:
Intervention Group (T-CPR):
Application of tourniquets to mechanically centralize blood volume (autotransfusion), in addition to all standard resuscitation measures according to current clinical guidelines.

Control Group:
Continuation of resuscitation according to current clinical standard without the use of tourniquets.

criteria:
Inclusion criteria:
Out-of-hospital cardiac arrest (OHCA)

Persistent/refractory cardiac arrest upon arrival in the emergency department, despite guideline-conform prehospital resuscitation efforts

Successful establishment of arterial access for invasive blood pressure monitoring in the emergency department

No contraindications to tourniquet application on the extremities
Exclusion criteria:
Successful ROSC prior to randomization

Known clinical or historical contraindications to tourniquet application (e.g., pre-existing severe peripheral arterial occlusive disease, amputations)

Severe traumatic injuries to the extremities that preclude safe tourniquet placement
